title: Credential Stuffing Risk
explanation: Reused credentials were observed together with a breach exposure. Attackers who obtain one leaked password routinely replay it against other services (credential stuffing), so the two findings compound rather than sitting independently.

title: Targeted Credential Theft
explanation: A likely phishing message was detected for an account whose identity (email/service) is already publicly exposed. Exposed identities give attackers the context to craft convincing, targeted lures.

title: Cascading Recovery Risk
explanation: A high-centrality account used as a recovery route for others shows signs of compromise. Because other accounts trust it for recovery, this can cascade across the dependency graph.

title: Elevated Takeover Risk
explanation: A breached account lacks a strong second factor. With no MFA, a leaked credential alone may be sufficient to reach the account, which raises severity above either finding alone.

title: Critical: MFA Ineffective Due to Session Exposure
explanation: A stolen session cookie that we assess as MFA bypass-capable means the attacker does not need to re-authenticate. MFA protects the login step, not an already-issued session, so the second factor is ineffective here. (This exposure scenario is SIMULATED — no real infostealer data is used.)

title: Reused Identity Across Breached and Safe Accounts
explanation: A breached account that also reuses passwords and lacks MFA combines the three factors most associated with account compromise into one path.

title: SIM-Swap Recovery Exposure
explanation: An account relies on SMS one-time codes for recovery while no stronger second factor is present. SMS is vulnerable to SIM-swap, so recovery can be subverted by porting the phone number.

title: Over-Permissioned Access Plus Active Phishing
explanation: A third-party app holds high-sensitivity permissions while phishing targeting the user is also detected. If the app or user is lured, the granted permissions widen what is exposed.
